subject_line: Into the Grey, and the road between Glin and Listowel
email_body:
Dear Mary,

I was reading about Into the Grey, your collection on dementia, and noticed that its proceeds go to Our Lady of Fatima Home in Tralee and Aras Mhuire in Listowel. I was also struck by Seven Steps to Birth a Crone, your collaboration with Rebecca Carroll and Susan Hitching that opened in Listowel in October 2023.

I'd love to ask how writing about dementia shaped the poems in Into the Grey, and what working alongside visual artists changed in your writing.

subject_line: From Heart and Bones to The Amendments, back in Kilkenny
email_body:
Dear Niamh,

I read the Kilkenny Observer piece on Heart and Bones: Love Songs for Late Youth, where you describe moving from Carlow to Kilkenny at eight and, more recently, coming home from the UK. Since then The Amendments has followed from Picador, with a Post Irish Book Award nomination.

I'd be curious to hear how the jump from stories to a novel felt, and whether returning to Kilkenny changed how you see the Ireland you write about.

subject_line: Sea hags, tarot and pole dancing in The Beautiful Afternoon
email_body:
Dear Airini,

The Beautiful Afternoon caught my eye for its range: history and literature sitting alongside Star Wars, sea hags, tarot, swimwear, environmentalism and pole dancing. I also noticed it was longlisted for the Ockham General Non-Fiction Prize in 2025, after years of poetry and short fiction often set in Whanganui.

I'd love to ask what the essay form lets you do that poems and stories don't, and how Whanganui finds its way into the essays.

subject_line: A colonial Wellington murder in Ōkiwi Brown
email_body:
Dear Cristina,

I came across Ōkiwi Brown, your historic murder set in Wellington from The Cuba Press, and noticed how it continues a line of historical fiction that includes Mrs Jewell and the wreck of the General Grant. Your Kete bio also mentions that you sail away on tall ships whenever you can, which made me wonder how that feeds the research.

I'd love to ask how you go from an archival scrap to a full scene, and what drew you to a Wellington murder.

subject_line: Caroline Herschel's wages in The Woman and Her Stars
email_body:
Dear Penny,

I've been looking at how your novels keep returning to real women who stepped into closed professions: Aleen Cust becoming the first woman vet in Britain and Ireland, Bertha Benz, Mary Leakey, and now Caroline Herschel in The Woman and Her Stars, who in 1787 became the first woman paid as an astronomer.

I'd love to ask how you choose each subject, and how your years as a journalist shape the line between record and invention.

subject_line: The Tjoa ash house on Green Hill
email_body:
Dear Audrey,

I was drawn to the premise of The Ash House: a nun sent to help a troubled heir in the Tjoa family's ash house on Kota Cahaya's Green Hill. Your blog describes the book as being about the plight of poor women in rich houses, told partly through two foreign domestic workers.

I'd love to ask why a ghost story felt like the right vehicle for those women, and how the sequel you've mentioned is taking shape.

subject_line: Two snakes from the Tang dynasty in Sister Snake
email_body:
Dear Amanda,

Sister Snake begins from a striking premise: Su, married to a conservative politician in Singapore, and Emerald, a sugar baby in New York, sisters whose shared history runs back to Tang dynasty China, when they were snakes. You rework The Legend of the White Snake around chosen family, queerness and passing.

I'd love to ask what the folktale gave you that a realist frame couldn't, and how you balanced the New York and Singapore halves of the book.

subject_line: The Havoc of Choice and Nairobi's public libraries
email_body:
Dear Wanjiru,

I've been reading about The Havoc of Choice, your debut novel, which became a national bestseller in Kenya and the UK between 2020 and 2022. What also stood out is that you co-founded Book Bunk, which renovates and runs some of Nairobi's best-known public libraries, so you're working on both the writing and the reading side of the city.

I'd love to ask how the library work and the fiction feed each other, and what Nairobi readers have told you about the novel.
